title: Women’s lived economic opportunity can lag formal legal equality, with gendered perception gaps revealing where rights are not felt in everyday work and care
source_unit: World Bank Women, Business and the Law and Gallup, Women's Lived Experience (W-LEX) Data
geography: Bangladesh, Brazil and Nigeria; nationally representative adult surveys collected in 2024

observations.period: July–December 2024; W-LEX pilot coverage and lived-opportunity measurement

denominator.unit: nationally representative adult respondents across Bangladesh, Brazil and Nigeria, approximately 1,000 per country

country_coverage.unit: countries included in the W-LEX pilot

survey_mode.value: face-to-face household interviews in local languages through the Gallup World Poll

topic_coverage.value: safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pension

measurement_purpose.value: measure how women's economic rights are experienced and perceived in everyday life

observations.method: World Bank WBL-Gallup supplemental survey modules integrated into the Gallup World Poll, with nationally representative adult samples in three countries.
observations.uncertainty: The pilot covers three countries and one collection period; nationally representative samples do not support global prevalence claims or causal attribution to specific laws.
observations.subgroup: Women and men in Bangladesh, Brazil and Nigeria, with comparisons across demographic and socioeconomic groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: A focused pilot can reveal implementation gaps that broad legal indices miss, while still requiring expansion across countries and repeated waves for trend inference.

observations.period: 2024; formal legal framework versus lived economic opportunity

denominator.unit: approximately 1,000 nationally representative respondents in each pilot country

brazil_legal_score.unit: Brazil WBL 2026 Legal Frameworks score out of 100

brazil_women_equal_pay.unit: percent of women in Brazil saying they receive equal pay

brazil_men_equal_pay.unit: percent of men in Brazil saying women receive equal pay

perception_gap.value: strong formal legal performance can coexist with large gendered gaps in perceived economic equality

observations.method: W-LEX comparison of Brazil's formal legal-framework score with first-person and third-person perceptions of equal pay.
observations.uncertainty: Perceptions of equal pay do not establish audited wage gaps, employer intent, legal violations or the causal role of Brazil's legal framework; the comparison is diagnostic.
observations.subgroup: Women and men in Brazil, workers, employers, policymakers and institutions responsible for pay transparency and enforcement.
observations.counterinterpretation: The perception gap may reflect different reference groups, information, norms or interpretation of equal pay rather than only enforcement failure.

denominator.unit: WBL topics combined in the W-LEX index

first_person_topics.unit: topics measuring women's own reported experience or perception

third_person_topics.value: pay, parenthood, childcare, assets, marriage and safety
third_person_topics.unit: topics measuring perceptions of broader societal conditions affecting women

index_scale.unit: maximum W-LEX country-level index score, with higher scores indicating more favorable perceived economic opportunity

observations.method: W-LEX index construction combining first-person perceptions of individual opportunity with third-person perceptions of social conditions and norms.
observations.uncertainty: The index combines distinct constructs and perceptions; it is not a direct measure of income, employment, violence, childcare use or legal compliance.
observations.subgroup: Women, men, households, workers, entrepreneurs and communities whose norms shape economic opportunity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Including perceived norms can reveal barriers that legal or administrative data miss, but norms and perceptions may change more slowly or differently than formal law.

implementation_signal.value: laws alone do not guarantee compliance or implementation; lived experience data can show where formal rights are not reflected in practice

norms_signal.value: perceived social norms can influence behavior and economic outcomes independently of formal laws

tracking_route.value: W-LEX is designed to expand to more countries and monitor whether legal reforms translate into real improvements over time

observations.method: World Bank policy-brief synthesis of W-LEX pilot data and intended complementarity with WBL legal, supportive-framework and enforcement-perception indicators.
observations.uncertainty: The expansion and longitudinal use are future plans; the pilot does not establish that W-LEX changes policy, predicts behavior or identifies causal mechanisms.
observations.subgroup: Women, policymakers, legal institutions, researchers, employers, civil society and data systems tracking gender equality.
observations.counterinterpretation: Better measurement can expose gaps, but measurement alone does not supply enforcement capacity, childcare, finance, safety or norm change.

related_sources.claim: Official W-LEX policy indicators brief and document record.
World Bank WBL framework and related 2026 legal, supportive and enforcement indicators.
W-LEX dataset, codebook and data access page.

boundary: This record is the lived-experience complement to the WBL 2026 legal benchmark. It uses nationally representative survey evidence from three countries, not a global survey, administrative wage records, a legal compliance audit, a causal evaluation or a measure of all women's economic experiences.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank W-LEX thematic page and policy-brief document record were reviewed for country coverage, sampling, survey mode, 10-topic index construction, Brazil equal-pay perception gaps and the law-to-practice monitoring purpose; the retrieved document page was hashed.
